facts.text: I'm a US service member.
Years ago I was deployed to East Africa.
For malaria prevention I took mefloquine 250 mg once a week, and I kept taking it for six months.
It started about two weeks after I began taking mefloquine, with anxiety and vivid dreams.

facts.item: how the symptoms progressed at first
facts.text: Over the next two months it progressed to problems with my balance and confusion.
I've been feeling anxious.
I have vivid dreams.
I became confused.
Four months into the deployment I came under enemy gunfire.

facts.item: change in symptoms after the gunfire
facts.text: My symptoms didn't change after that event.
Since I came back I've had mood swings; I get angry and irritable.
I have trouble concentrating.
I don't enjoy things the way I used to.
My short-term memory has gotten bad.
I have trouble finding the right words.

facts.item: feeling of being on a boat
facts.text: I have persistent "sea legs", a feeling as if I'm on a boat.
I get attacks of vertigo.
They come 4 to 5 times a day.
Each one lasts 20 to 30 minutes.
Closing my eyes helps.
Apart from the spinning, the attacks don't bring on any other bodily symptoms.
On top of the attacks, I feel a constant spinning dizziness.
I've been falling.
I have trouble sleeping.
I have nightmares.
I get headaches every day.
I don't get an aura before them.
Light doesn't bother me during the headaches.
I haven't had any significant environmental exposures.
I don't use illicit drugs.
I've never had a head injury.
I drank alcohol during the deployment, but since then I've kept it limited.
A psychiatrist diagnosed me with anxiety.
A psychiatrist diagnosed me with PTSD.
The treatment for my anxiety and PTSD made my mood somewhat better, but the balance problems and the sleep problems haven't improved.
I've been treated with prazosin.
I've been treated with clonazepam.
I've been treated with lorazepam.
I've been treated with venlafaxine.
I've been treated with diazepam.
I've been treated with clonidine.
I've had psychotherapy.

findings.name: gait and balance
findings.result: Loss of balance on rising and on tandem gait.

findings.name: neurological examination
findings.result: Normal, except for loss of balance on rising and on tandem gait.

findings.name: MRI of the brain and internal auditory canals
vestibular testing
findings.result: Hyperactive vestibulo-ocular reflex gains and abnormally low phase on rotary chair testing, consistent with a central vestibulopathy.

gold.reasoning: 1. Mal de debarquement syndrome considered due to persistent disequilibrium after sea travel — “The differential diagnosis includes persistent PTSD and mal de debarquement syndrome.” 2. Chronic subjective dizziness considered among somatoform disorders but less likely given vestibular test abnormalities — “The documented history of significant vestibular dysfunction as evidenced by the abnormal findings on vestibular testing are more consistent with mefloquine toxicity rather than PTSD or somatoform disorders such as chronic subjective dizziness.”

f006: Anxiety is reported at onset (s001) and later diagnosed by psychiatry (s006); the symptom and the diagnosis are separate facts. Whether it is current is not stated beyond 'partial improvement in mood'.
f008: Confusion is reported only during the early course (s001); whether it persists is not stated, so no time is given.
f016: Combines the early 'disequilibrium' (s001) with the persistent 'sea legs' on return (s003).
f021: 'Without autonomic symptoms' is written as a scoped blanket denial; specific autonomic symptoms are not named in the source.
f036: Whether each psychiatric medicine is current or past is not stated, so no time is given (same for f037-f041).

leakage.reason: The patient knows the name of the antimalarial he took; the drug history is the core of the case.
The symptom onset is told relative to starting mefloquine, as in the source; the patient knows this timeline.

source_issues: The source says 'consistent with a central vestibulopathy' inside the vestibular test result; kept as the report's conclusion.
notes: Index visit: the referral evaluation for chronic neuropsychiatric and vestibular symptoms years after deployment (s001-s011); the deployment, mefloquine course, earlier symptoms and the psychiatric diagnoses and treatments are history the patient reports at this visit.
Earlier psychiatric diagnoses (anxiety, PTSD) and their treatments are facts because the patient was told and treated before the index visit; the treatment response is a child of the PTSD fact.
Psychotherapy is filed as medical_history (a treatment that is not a medicine).
Opening: the referral complaints, represented by the persistent sea legs and vertigo attacks (vestibular) and the mood swings (neuropsychiatric).
